decision.conviction_status: The conviction of Salim Shamsuddin Shaikh (A-2) is set aside. The conviction of Mohmed Rafiq Abdul Rahim Shaikh (A-4) under Section 25 (1) (a) & 25 (1AA) read with Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959 is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of an accused under Sections 25(1)(a) and 25(1AA) of the Arms Act, 1959 can be sustained based on constructive possession, merely because they are the registered owner of the vehicle (A-2) or the recorded occupier of the premises (A-4) from where arms/ammunition were recovered, without the prosecution proving conscious possession or control.

facts: Live cartridges were found in a car driven by accused A-1.
Accused A-2 was the registered owner of this car but was not present in or near the vehicle when it was apprehended.
A-2 was arrested solely because he was the owner of the car.
Based on a disclosure by A-1, more weapons and ammunition were found in the cellar of a house.
Accused A-4 was the recorded occupier of this house.
However, A-4 had been in detention for almost three months prior to the recovery and was not in physical possession or occupation of the house.
law: To establish an offense under Section 25(1)(a) of the Arms Act, the prosecution must prove "conscious possession."
Conscious possession requires the element of intention, consciousness, or knowledge of the firearm.
Possession can be "constructive," which means having power and control over the firearm, even without physical possession.
To prove constructive possession, it is necessary to show that the accused had control over the place where the items were found or had placed them there.
Mere ownership of a vehicle or recorded occupancy of a premises is not, by itself, sufficient to prove conscious or constructive possession.
application: For accused A-2 (the car owner), the court found no evidence of conscious possession. He was not in the car, and the prosecution's case rested entirely on the fact that he was the registered owner. The court held that this was insufficient to prove he had knowledge or control over the cartridges found inside.

For accused A-4 (the house occupier), the court found that he could not have been in constructive possession of the weapons. Since he had been in detention for three months, he was not in control of the house. The prosecution failed to present any evidence to establish A-4's intention or consciousness regarding the arms and ammunition found in the cellar.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the convictions of A-2 and A-4 were not sustainable. The court rejected the idea that constructive possession could be established merely from the fact of being the registered owner of a vehicle (A-2) or the recorded occupier of a premises (A-4). The prosecution must prove that the accused had conscious possession, meaning they had knowledge of and control over the arms or ammunition. Since the prosecution failed to provide such proof for either accused, their convictions were overturned.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, which presumes liability for persons in joint occupation or control of any premises or vehicle, can be applied to sustain a conviction when the prosecution fails to establish conscious possession or control by the accused.

facts: Accused A-2 was the registered owner of a car from which live cartridges were recovered. However, A-2 was not in or near the car at the time of its apprehension; another accused, A-1, was driving it.
Accused A-4 was the recorded occupier of a house where weapons and cartridges were found in a cellar.
At the time of the recovery and for nearly three months prior, A-4 had been in jail and was therefore not in physical possession or occupation of the house.
law: Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, presumes liability for persons in joint occupation or control of a premises/vehicle where arms are found, but only if there is "reason to believe" that the person was "aware of the existence of the arms".

A fundamental precondition for an offense under the Arms Act (specifically Section 25(1)(a)) is the element of "conscious possession," which involves intention, consciousness, or knowledge of the firearm.
Possession can be physical or constructive. Constructive possession requires proof that the accused had power and control over the weapon, even if not in physical possession.
To sustain a conviction, the prosecution must prove that the accused was in conscious possession at some point and retained control over the object at the time of recovery.
application: Regarding A-2 (the car owner), the court found that the prosecution failed to establish that he was in joint control or occupation of the car with A-1 at the time of the incident. Convicting him based solely on ownership, without any evidence of his knowledge or control over the cartridges, was deemed unsustainable. The lower courts had not even made a finding of constructive possession.

Regarding A-4 (the house occupier), the court determined it was impossible to hold him in "joint occupation" under Section 35 because he was in jail. The prosecution failed to establish the necessary intention and consciousness on his part regarding the weapons found in the house.
The court also rejected the argument of constructive possession for A-4, as there was no proof that he had placed the weapons there or was in control of the house, given his detention.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the application of the presumption under Section 35 of the Arms Act, holding that it cannot be used to sustain a conviction when the prosecution fails to establish the fundamental prerequisite of conscious possession. The court clarified that Section 35 does not create automatic liability based on ownership or occupation alone; the prosecution must first prove that the accused had knowledge, awareness, and control (either actual or constructive) over the arms or ammunition. Since this essential element was not proven for either A-2 or A-4, their convictions were overturned.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of an accused under Sections 25(1)(a) and 25(1AA) of the Arms Act, 1959 can be sustained based on constructive possession, merely because they are the registered owner of the vehicle (A-2) or the recorded occupier of the premises (A-4) from where arms/ammunition were recovered, without the prosecution proving conscious possession or control.
appellant_arguments: Mere registered ownership of a vehicle is insufficient to establish conscious possession or control over arms found within it.
The accused (A-2) was not physically present in or near the car when it was apprehended, which negates actual possession.
The accused, a car broker, had given the car to another person (A-1) who was interested in purchasing it, thus he was not in control of the vehicle.
The prosecution failed to prove the essential element of conscious possession, and the lower courts erred by convicting solely on the basis of ownership.
respondent_arguments: The accused (A-2) was the registered owner of the car from which the arms and ammunition were recovered.
Registered ownership is a sufficient basis to establish constructive possession and liability for illegal items found within the vehicle.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, which presumes liability for persons in joint occupation or control of any premises or vehicle, can be applied to sustain a conviction when the prosecution fails to establish conscious possession or control by the accused.
appellant_arguments: The presumption of liability under Section 35 cannot be invoked based on ownership alone, particularly when the owner was not in actual occupation or control of the vehicle at the relevant time.
The prosecution must first establish the foundational fact of conscious possession or control before the presumption under Section 35 can be applied.
respondent_arguments: As the registered owner, the accused is presumed to be in control of the vehicle under Section 35.
This presumption of control makes the owner liable for the arms found inside, shifting the burden to the accused to prove they had no knowledge or control.

cases.case_name: Gunwantlal vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: The text states that the Court relied on a holding from Para 5 of this case, but the specific legal principle is not quoted in the provided text.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction under Section 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, cannot be sustained on the grounds that it renders each of several people in joint occupation or control of any premises, vehicle, or other place liable as if they committed the offense alone.
obiter: The offense under Section 25 (1) (a) & 25 (1AA) of the Arms Act, 1959 shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A conviction under the Arms Act cannot be sustained based on constructive possession derived merely from the accused's status as the registered owner of a vehicle. The prosecution must prove the essential element of possession. Furthermore, the presumption of liability under Section 35 of the Arms Act cannot be applied where the prosecution fails to even allege, let alone prove, the foundational requirement of joint control or occupation of the vehicle.
legal_tests_applied: For a conviction under Section 25 (1AA) of the Arms Act, the prosecution must prove that the accused was in possession of the prohibited ammunition.

To sustain a conviction under Section 35 of the Arms Act, it must be the prosecution's case that the accused were found in 'joint control or occupation' of the vehicle from which the prohibited items were recovered.
